items.title: Carbs per Gram
items.question: Roughly how many Calories does one gram of carbohydrate provide?
items.correctExplanation: About 4. Carbohydrate and protein share the same energy density per gram.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Knowing the per-gram values for each macronutrient makes label reading quick.
items.lessonContent:
Each macronutrient has a known energy density.
Per-gram values make label maths fast.
Compare foods by composition, not just weight.
Small densities still add up over a day.
Share this: estimate the energy in one snack from its macronutrients.

items.title: Protein per Gram
items.question: One gram of protein supplies roughly how much energy to the body?
items.correctExplanation: About 4. Protein matches carbohydrate in energy density despite its different role.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Protein's main job is building tissue, but its energy content per gram equals carbohydrate's.
items.lessonContent:
Function and energy density are separate facts.
Two nutrients can share a density but differ in role.
Compare roles, not just calories.
Use per-gram values for quick estimates.
Share this: compare the roles of two foods with the same energy density.

items.title: Fat per Gram
items.question: How much energy does a single gram of fat supply?
items.correctExplanation: About 9. This nutrient carries more than twice the energy of carbohydrate or protein per gram.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Its high density explains why small amounts contribute large shares of a meal's energy.
items.lessonContent:
Energy density varies widely between nutrients.
High density means small portions matter.
Read composition, not just portion size.
Compare densities before judging a food.
Share this: check the density of one food you eat daily.

items.title: Alcohol per Gram
items.question: Pure alcohol supplies roughly how much energy per gram?
items.correctExplanation: About 7. Alcohol sits between carbohydrate and fat in energy density.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Its energy is easy to overlook because drinks are not always thought of as food.
items.lessonContent:
Not all energy sources appear on a plate.
Drinks can carry substantial energy.
Check what is easy to overlook.
Density tells you how much a small amount adds.
Share this: estimate the energy in one drink you might overlook.

items.title: Kilogram of Fat
items.question: Roughly how many Calories must be removed to lose one kilogram of body fat tissue?
items.correctExplanation: About 7700. Fat tissue is not pure energy, so the figure is lower than the raw density suggests.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7700. Tissue contains water and other material, so the energy cost per kilogram is not simply nine times a thousand.
items.lessonContent:
Body tissue is a mixture, not a pure fuel.
Real-world figures differ from raw density.
Spread large deficits over time.
Check assumptions behind a rule of thumb.
Share this: plan one realistic weekly deficit instead of a crash.

items.title: Mile of Running
items.question: Roughly how many Calories does an average adult burn running one mile?
items.correctExplanation: About 100. The cost scales with body weight and distance more than with speed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 100. Distance and weight dominate, which is why fast and slow runners over the same mile differ little.
items.lessonContent:
Energy cost tracks distance and mass.
Speed changes time, not the total much.
Estimate exercise cost from distance.
Compare effort with the food it offsets.
Share this: estimate the energy of one walk or run you take.

items.title: Thirty Percent Fat
items.question: On a 2000-Calorie daily diet, how many Calories come from fat at thirty percent?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 600. Thirty percent of two thousand is six hundred Calories.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 600. Multiplying the total by the fraction gives the share quickly.
items.lessonContent:
Percentages convert to amounts easily.
Know the total before taking a share.
Fractions and percentages are interchangeable.
Check the share against portion sizes.
Share this: compute one percentage of your daily energy target.

items.title: Energy Currency
items.question: What molecule do cells use as their immediate energy currency?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Cells spend this molecule to power almost every process.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ATP. It is the rechargeable unit cells exchange for work of all kinds.
items.lessonContent:
Cells need a spendable form of energy.
One molecule serves as the common currency.
Energy is stored and released in small packets.
Biological systems reuse a standard unit.
Share this: think of one daily system that runs on a common unit.

items.title: Cellular Burning
items.question: What is the process called by which cells release energy from glucose using oxygen?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Cells combine glucose with oxygen to release usable energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cellular respiration. It is a slow, controlled release rather than a flame, which is why it powers life without burning tissue.
items.lessonContent:
Energy release can be controlled, not explosive.
Oxygen enables a more complete breakdown.
Waste products must be expelled.
Chemistry inside cells mirrors combustion safely.
Share this: notice one process that releases energy slowly and safely.

items.title: Long Slow Effort
items.question: What kind of exercise relies on oxygen over sustained periods, such as jogging or cycling?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Sustained effort that uses oxygen steadily builds endurance.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is aerobic exercise. Because oxygen is available throughout, this work can continue for a long time.
items.lessonContent:
Fuelling method shapes endurance.
With oxygen, effort can be steady and long.
Without it, bursts are short.
Match the activity to the energy system.
Share this: pick one long, steady activity for this week.

items.title: Short Hard Effort
items.question: What kind of exercise is intense and brief, working faster than oxygen can be supplied?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Very intense effort outstrips oxygen supply and can only be sustained briefly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is anaerobic exercise. Its intensity is its limit, since the body cannot keep it up for long.
items.lessonContent:
Intensity and duration trade against each other.
Some efforts outrun oxygen delivery.
Bursts give way to recovery.
Choose the mode that fits your goal.
Share this: try one short, intense burst followed by rest.

items.title: Stored Muscle Fuel
items.question: What form of stored carbohydrate do muscles and the liver keep for quick energy?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. This branched storage form of glucose can be broken down quickly when demand rises.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is glycogen. It is the body's fast-access reserve, unlike fat which releases energy more slowly.
items.lessonContent:
Storage forms enable quick access.
Different reserves serve different speeds.
Bodies stockpile for predictable demand.
Refuel before and after hard effort.
Share this: plan one meal around an upcoming demanding activity.

items.title: Burning Muscles
items.question: What substance builds up and causes the burning feeling during very hard exercise?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Intense effort produces this byproduct faster than it can be cleared, contributing to the burn.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is lactic acid. It accumulates during hard work and dissipates with rest and oxygen.
items.lessonContent:
Byproducts signal the limits of a process.
Hard effort outpaces clearing mechanisms.
Recovery restores balance.
Sensations are information about metabolism.
Share this: notice how one intense effort eases with rest.

items.title: Label Unit
items.question: Food labels use a 'Calorie' that is technically what larger unit?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The dietary unit equals a thousand small calories of physics.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a kilocalorie. The everyday name is a shortened form of the larger scientific unit.
items.lessonContent:
Common names can hide precise units.
A factor of a thousand changes meaning.
Read definitions before comparing numbers.
Units are part of the claim.
Share this: check the exact unit on one label or meter.

items.title: Resting Burn
items.question: What does basal metabolic rate measure, in plain terms?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. It is the energy the body spends at complete rest just to stay alive.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is resting energy use. Even without movement, organs and cells consume energy continuously.
items.lessonContent:
Bodies spend energy even at rest.
Baseline needs anchor daily estimates.
Most energy use happens below awareness.
Distinguish resting cost from activity.
Share this: estimate what your body burns without moving.

items.title: Eating Less
items.question: What is the gradual result of consistently taking in less energy than you use?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A sustained gap between intake and use draws on stored reserves.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is weight loss. The change follows the arithmetic over time, not any single day.
items.lessonContent:
Direction follows the energy balance.
Single days matter less than trends.
Slow changes are more sustainable.
Track the trend, not the day.
Share this: compare one week's intake and activity honestly.

items.title: Eating More
items.question: What usually follows from a lasting excess of intake over use?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A sustained surplus is stored, mostly as reserve tissue.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is weight gain. The body banks the difference rather than discarding it.
items.lessonContent:
Surplus energy is stored, not discarded.
Storage happens gradually.
Trends beat single meals.
Balance awareness prevents drift.
Share this: notice one small daily surplus that could add up.

items.title: Building Blocks
items.question: What is the main role of protein in the body, beyond providing energy?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Protein supplies the raw material for muscles, organs, and repair.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is building tissue. Its structural role matters more than the energy it can eventually yield.
items.lessonContent:
Nutrients have primary roles.
Structure and fuel are different functions.
Prioritise building over burning.
Match intake to the job a nutrient does.
Share this: name one food that supports repair rather than quick energy.

items.title: Vitamin Carrier
items.question: Which dietary component helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. These vitamins dissolve in fat, so some fat in a meal improves their absorption.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is dietary fat. Without it, fat-soluble vitamins pass through largely unused.
items.lessonContent:
Some nutrients need a carrier to absorb.
Solubility determines how vitamins travel.
Balance matters more than elimination.
Pair nutrients for better uptake.
Share this: check whether one healthy food is paired with a helpful carrier.

items.title: Body Heat
items.question: During exercise, most of the energy released from fuel is eventually lost as what?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Only a fraction becomes mechanical work; the rest escapes as warmth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is heat loss. Inefficiency in energy conversion is why exercise raises body temperature.
items.lessonContent:
Conversion is never perfectly efficient.
Wasted energy usually appears as warmth.
Inefficiency explains physical sensations.
Track where the remainder goes.
Share this: notice one process that warms things as a byproduct.

items.title: Exercise Alone
items.question: Why does exercise by itself often fail to produce large weight changes?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A typical session burns far less than most people assume compared with daily intake.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is small energy cost. Exercise brings many benefits, but its direct energy use is modest relative to eating.
items.lessonContent:
Effort and energy cost are not identical.
Perceived exertion can overstate expenditure.
Combine activity with intake changes.
Measure rather than assume.
Share this: compare one workout's cost with one snack's energy.

items.title: Stored Surplus
items.question: In what form does the body mainly store long-term surplus energy?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Fat is the body's dense, long-term energy reserve, packed efficiently for storage.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is body fat. It holds far more energy per gram than the short-term reserves used during exercise.
items.lessonContent:
Long-term storage favours dense forms.
Different reserves serve different durations.
Storage efficiency matters for survival.
Balance intake with use over time.
Share this: name one long-term reserve you maintain.

items.title: Lab Measurement
items.question: What laboratory technique measures a food's energy content by burning it completely?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The sample is combusted in a sealed vessel and the released heat is measured.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bomb calorimetry. It captures all the energy a food contains, which is more than the body can extract.
items.lessonContent:
Measurement methods shape reported values.
Complete combustion overstates usable energy.
Distinguish what a food holds from what is absorbed.
Question how a number was obtained.
Share this: ask how one nutritional figure was actually measured.

items.title: Richest Fuel
items.question: Which macronutrient supplies the most energy per gram?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. At about nine Calories per gram it exceeds both carbohydrate and protein.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is fat. Its density is why even small amounts of rich foods carry substantial energy.
items.lessonContent:
Energy density differs by nutrient.
Dense sources need smaller portions.
Composition matters as much as quantity.
Compare per-gram values before judging.
Share this: compare the density of two foods you often eat.

items.title: Fibre per Gram
items.question: How much energy does a gram of dietary fibre actually deliver?
items.correctExplanation: About 2. Fibre resists full digestion, so it yields far less energy than other carbohydrates.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Because it is not fully broken down, its contribution is small and often counted separately.
items.lessonContent:
Not everything eaten is absorbed.
Digestibility changes energy yield.
Count resistant components differently.
Expect lower values from fibre-rich foods.
Share this: note one food whose energy is only partly available.
